title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 250
paragraphs: Of Egypt, however, I shall give a full report, because it has more wonders than any other land, and its works too are as great beyond expression as any land has to show. For this reason, then, more shall be said about it.

The Egyptians, in keeping with their climate which is unlike any other, and with their river which shows a nature different from all other rivers, have established for themselves manners and customs that are, in almost all matters, opposite to those of other men. Among them the women go to market and carry on trade, while the men remain at home and weave; and whereas others weave by pushing the woof upwards, the Egyptians push it downwards. The men carry burdens on their heads, the women on their shoulders. The women urinate standing up, the men crouching down. They relieve themselves in their houses and eat outside in the streets, giving as their reason that one should do in secret what is unseemly though necessary, and in public what is not unseemly. No woman is priestess of any divinity, male or female; men serve as priests of all, both male and female. The sons are in no way compelled to support their parents if they do not desire to do so, but the daughters are forced to, however unwilling they may be.
